1.title: The Lantern in the Dorm
1.cn: 转学生米拉在寄宿学校的第一周：从一只旧灯笼开始，她慢慢读懂新学校的节奏、规则与温度。

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · A Typical Day, Minus the Ordinary
chapters.text:
On her first night in the **dorm**, Mira lay awake until **midnight**. The **digital** clock on her desk flashed 00:00, and a small **lantern** her grandmother had given her glowed on the shelf. It was a **unique** object in a room full of standard furniture, and it reminded her of home.

It was a **typical** morning: she stepped **onto** the bus, thinking about two **related** questions. Her **routine** at the new school was still a mystery. The **schedule** on her phone listed a **conference** with her **senior** mentor at nine, a **junior** class meeting at ten, and a **volunteer** **event** in the afternoon. The school was a large **organization** with a **quality** reputation, and every **aspect** of its **behaviour** code seemed designed to **inspire** **respect**.

"Your only **goal** this week," her **partner** Theo said at breakfast, "is to **acquire** one good habit." Theo had a **particular** **attitude** toward **tradition**: he **reflect**ed on it, questioned it, but never dismissed it.

Mira **select**ed a **type** of tea from the machine, pressed the **button**, and watched the water **deliver** itself into her cup. **Currently**, the school was trying to **improve** its **electricity** use, so the machine switched off after each cup. A small **tip** printed on the **material** beside it explained why.

At the **conference**, the mentor asked each student to **respond** to one question: what do you want to **earn** here? Mira wrote: a **description** of myself that I can trust. The mentor smiled. "That is a fine **challenge**," she said. "And a fine **element** of any **exploration**."

After class, Mira helped **edit** the notice board for the volunteer event. The **location** was the old gym, and the **length** of the walk there surprised her. On the way she passed a **scene** she would remember: two **senior** students teaching a **junior** one to fold paper lanterns, their hands moving with the ease of long practice.

That night, the **death** of the clock's battery left the room dark, and Mira laughed. She had come here for **freedom**, and here it was: a small room, a dead clock, a living lantern, and a **routine** she was beginning to **improve**, one ordinary day at a time.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · A Million Stones, One View
chapters.text:
On Saturday the whole class set off for a **historic** **site** outside the city. The **destination** was a **former** royal **court**, **originally** built as a **defence** against invaders. **Nowadays** it is a museum, and more than a **million** visitors walk through its **entrance** every year.

"It looks **amazing** in photos," said Theo, "but the **structure** is what interests me." He pointed at the **sculpture** in the courtyard: a **statue** of a general holding a **weapon** that had never been used in a real **battle**. "That is not a **feature** of war," he said. "It is a **memory** of fear."

Mira opened her **blog** and began to **chat** about the **view**. From the top of the wall, the **desert** stretched **nowhere** in particular, and the **crowded** streets of **downtown** seemed far away. For a **moment** she felt **embarrassed** by her own **opinion** — that old stones could be **energetic** — but she wrote it down anyway.

Their guide, a **former** teacher, explained the **origin** of the **poetry** carved on the wall. "These lines were the **basis** of a whole **scientific** tradition," she said. "They **contribute** to our understanding of the stars." Mira began to **admire** the care behind each line; she could **indicate** exactly where the stone had been repaired, and she **vote**d to spend the rest of the trip there.

In the afternoon, the class was given an **opportunity** to **settle** a small **dispute** about **transport**. Some students wanted to walk; others preferred the bus. "Let us put it in an **envelope** and decide later," said the guide, laughing. **Afterwards**, they all agreed that the walk had been the real **adventure**. Mira did not **fancy** another long walk, but she was glad she had come.

Back at school, Mira tried to **position** her photos on the **blog**, but the page kept moving. She was **shocked** at how much she had written — and **altogether** happy with it. The trip had **disappoint**ed no one.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · The Label on the Fridge
chapters.text:
The next **challenge** was the **convenience** store by the **facility** gate. Mira had never read a food **label** before; she simply grabbed a **snack** and threw the **packaging** away. Then a **teenager** in her class, Lena, asked her a question that changed her **routine**: "Do you know where the **plastic** **container** goes?"

Lena was a **consumer** with strong opinions. She had done a project on the **global** food system, and she could **prove** that a single **amount** of wasted food released a surprising amount of **greenhouse** **gas**. "Every choice has an **impact**," she said. "**Moreover**, the **details** matter."

They stood in front of the fridge, where **frozen** food sat beside **yoghurt** and **pudding**. "A **slim** figure on the **image** is not a health plan," Lena went on. "**Actually**, most **diet** advice for **teenagers** comes from people who want to sell something." She pointed to the **source** of a claim on a poster and asked Mira to **comment** on it.

Mira began to **tend** to agree. She did not want to **assume** anything without evidence, and she wanted to **establish** a few rules for herself. Could the school **legally** **permit** students to bring their own **container**? Could the store **recycle** more and install an **energy-efficient** fridge? The manager, a **retired** teacher, listened carefully and did not **stress** the rules; instead he offered a **link** to the city's recycling guide.

"**Despite** the **loss** of a few customers," he said, "we can do better. We can **determine** what sells and what is wasted, and we can make the **cattle** and the **groceries** part of one honest system." He asked Mira to **remind** him of the meeting and to **apologize** to no one for asking.

At lunch, the class held a debate. Mira had to **host** one table, and she had to keep the discussion **equal** — every voice, including the quietest **junior**, should count. She did not **fancy** public speaking, but she **prove**d to herself that she could do it. By the end, the **expert** from the city office said the students had made a real **impact**. The **decoration** on the wall — a painted **label** saying "Choose well" — suddenly looked less like **decoration** and more like advice.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · A Room with a Soul
chapters.text:
Mira's **apartment** at home had been small, but her **dorm** room was smaller. On the first **occasion** she had time to **arrange** it, she stood on a chair and looked at the **ceiling**, then at the **narrow** bed, the **curtain**, and the **poster** she had **intended** to put up. The room was **extremely** plain, and she **prefer**red it that way — for now.

Her **goal** was a **labour-saving** room. She bought a small **device** that could **download** her **files** and **software** updates, and a lamp that switched itself off. **Unfortunately**, the **company** that made the lamp had gone out of business, and the **brochure** promised more than the lamp could do. She did not **argue** with it, and she did not want to **suffer** in silence; she simply **grab**bed a screwdriver and fixed the switch.

The **experiment** of living alone was harder than she had expected. She had to **boil** water for tea, **load** the washing machine, and **regularly** check that the **petrol** heater was off. A **percentage** of her **data** disappeared when the Wi-Fi dropped, and a **bomb** of homesickness hit her on the second night. "You are **capable** of more than you think," her mother said on the phone. "**Definitely**."

Her **senior** friend Theo had a **talent** for turning a room into a **time-honoured** place. He brought a small **piano** **downstairs** — with the **goods** lift, since the stairs were too **narrow** — and played while Mira **gather**ed her **stuff**. "Music is a **technique** for **survive**ing," he said. "It **decrease**s the noise in your head."

On the wall, Mira put a photo of her grandmother's house, an **upper-class** home from the 1940s with a **style** all its own. "Every **adult** I know wants a bigger room," she said. "I want a room with a **soul**." She **recommend**ed the same **aim** to her **partner**: choose one thing that will last, and let the rest **disappear**. **Immediately** after she said it, the lamp flickered, and they both laughed. **Slightly** embarrassed, she **load**ed the photo **file** again and set it as her screen. The room, at last, had a **style** of its own — and a **responsibility** to match.

2.title: The Risk Report
2.cn: 萨姆和艾达做一份关于“冒险”的课题报告：从安全带、滑雪到冲浪事故，他们逐渐明白风险、判断与成就的关系。

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · Blame the Brain?
chapters.text:
Sam had always been a careful boy, the kind who fastens his **seat belt** before the engine starts and reads every **section** of the safety card. So when his teacher announced the **theme** of the term — "No limits" — he felt a familiar **pressure** in his chest.

"You need a **strategy**," said Ada, his **partner** on the project. "Pick one **issue**, one **factor** that changes how people take risks, and study it properly." Ada was **independent** and **ambitious**; she had already written to a **charity** that studied a rare **disease** of the nervous system. Her **confidence** did not **impress** Sam. It **frightened** him a little, and a **frightening** idea followed: what if she was right?

Their first interview was with a former **adventurer** named Ruth, who had once tried to **ski** across a **continent** and had the **boot** to prove it. "People **blame** the brain for every bad **judgement**," Ruth said. "But a **chemical** signal is not a **solution**. It is only a **factor**." She showed them a **statistic**: most accidents happen to people who believe they are **reliable** judges of their own **limit**.

Sam began to **conduct** his own **attempt** to measure risk. He built a small **vehicle** with a **limited** range and a sensor that could **contain** a **reaction** time test. The results were **incredible**: students who said they were **responsible** were not always the fastest to **adapt**. "**To what extent**," Ada asked, "does **curiosity** change the **account**?"

The answer came from an **eyewitness** at the **base** of the mountain: a **native** guide who had watched a **surfing** accident from the shore. She could **reveal** exactly what went wrong, and she did not **blame** the young man. "He was **dizzy** from the cold," she said. "**Preserve** the story, not the shame."

The **author** of their report turned out to be Sam himself. He wrote the final **section** in one sitting, and for the first time he felt that his **achievement** was not a **limit** he had avoided, but one he had chosen. "I want to **quit** being afraid of fear," he told Ada. She smiled. "That is an **issue** worth a whole **series**."

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · One Episode at a Time
chapters.text:
The school launched an **experiment**: every class would produce one **episode** of a podcast **series** about learning. Sam and Ada were given the **previous** year's recordings and a **brief** from the head teacher: keep it **positive**, keep it **brief**, and **quote** real students.

Their first job was to **document** the school's **resources**. The library had a **lecture** room, a recording studio, and a **supply** of old microphones. "We are **eager** to help," said the librarian, who **frequently** **update**d the notice board. "**Otherwise**," she added, "nobody knows what we have."

The theme of their episode was **motivate** — how to keep a good **mood** when exams approach. They interviewed a **devoted** teacher who used **creative** tasks and a **performance** night to to give students a sense of **satisfaction**. "A **positive** **effect** on **concentration** is **obviously** worth the effort," she said. "But you must **recognize** that **cooperation** takes practice, and that **mental** health is not a **debate**."

Then a **hurricane** hit the **county**. It tore a **path** through the **valley**, and the school became a centre for **aid**. Students **donate**d clothes and food; the **supply** of water was **tight** for two days. "We need a **procedure**," Ada said, "and we need everyone to be **aware** of it." The head teacher asked Sam to **summarize** the plan, to **propose** a rota for the volunteers, and to **promote** it on the school **Wi-Fi** page. A charity for **cancer** research sent a thank-you card.

That week, a **major** **accident** on the coast road made the news: a small boat had tried to **sail** into the **ocean** and had lost its **signal**. The **audience** for their podcast grew. "**Indeed**, we are **addicted** to our phones," one student said on air, "but the **benefit** of a real conversation is that it can **prevent** a bad decision."

The episode ended with a **quote** from the **master** of the school: "**Academic** success is not a **cure** for loneliness, and a **uniform** is not an **identity**." The class **clap**ped. Sam felt the **function** of the project change: it was no longer about grades. "Let us **pursue** this," he said. "**Series** two starts next week."

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · A Letter That Travelled
chapters.text:
For the third **episode**, the team turned to a bigger **range** of questions. A **billion** people, the **figure** went, would be affected by a **climate** that was changing at an **alarming** **rate**. "Can we **predict** the next **chain** reaction?" Ada asked.

Their science teacher was **concerned** but calm. "**Agriculture** and **hunting** both **threaten** species with **extinction**," she said. "**Somehow**, the **youth** of today must **admit** that **unfamiliar** facts are not the enemy." She asked them to **measure** what they could and to **imply** nothing they had not tested.

Sam wrote a **formal** letter to a **major** **official** at the city's environment office, asking for an interview. To his surprise, the answer came by **exchange** of emails: a **fluent** young officer invited them to a **range** of meetings. "**Madam**," Sam began, then stopped. "**Therefore**," he wrote instead, "we would be **grateful** if you could **advertise** our **advertisement** — sorry, our campaign — to your **contact** list."

The officer laughed when she read it. "**Absolutely** no problem," she said. "But let me **contrast** two **options**: a **fund** for local **design** projects, or a **balance** between **available** **resources**. Which do you **desire**?" The team chose the second, and promised to **reduce** waste **plus** report every **process** honestly.

That spring, a **graduate** student showed them how to test a **cloth** **net** against **mud** and **string** in a **mirror** of the local river. "We must **tear** down the old **figure** of the **youth** who does not care," she said. "**Eventually**, the **concerned** will **fund** the work." A **flight** over the delta showed the **official** how much had changed **significantly** in a decade.

Sam wrote back **faithfully** — a word Ada teased him for — and signed the letter **formally**. In the final **episode** of the series, the **range** of voices was wider than ever: a farmer, a student, an officer, a scientist. "We are not **concerned** about blame any more," Sam said. "We are **concerned** about the next **measure**."

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · The Old Man and the Net
chapters.text:
The last chapter took Sam to a fishing village his grandfather had left **a decade** ago. The **atmosphere** was salt and rope and **grain** dust. An old fisherman named Elias agreed to take him out, on one **request**: no camera, no **title**, just work.

"You want to **gain** a story," Elias said. "Then **maintain** the line and do not **attack** the sea." He showed Sam how to **wrap** the rope around a **brick** to keep the **net** steady, how to **approach** a **shark** without **bleed**ing, and how to read a **sharp** change in the **sky** by the colour of the water.

They set out before dawn. The boat was small but **self-sufficient**, with a **professional** **target**: enough fish for the village, no more. "**Curious** animals are not a **threat**," Elias said. "**Intelligent** ones are." A **bite** on the line, a **struggle** on the deck, and then a **shark** that **attacked** the catch and **destroy**ed the net. Sam felt the boat **sink** slightly and his confidence with it. The smell of the catch would **attract** gulls for hours.

"A **setback**," Elias said, "is not a **failure**. **Realistic** men **lack** nothing but **luck**." He took a **clue** from the wind and changed course. By noon they had **outstanding** **strength** in their arms and a **shortage** of nothing. The village **institute** later gave Elias a **medal** for fifty years at sea.

Sam wrote the final script that night. The **title** was simple: *The Old Man and the Net*. His teacher said the ending was **false** — too happy. Sam **defeat**ed the doubt by adding a line: "**Ahead** of us the weather changed **dramatically**, and we turned back." He chose to leave the **literature** of the sea unfinished, and he **permanently** kept the **brick** on his desk as a paperweight, a **clue** to what he had learned. **Skin** and **bone**, he wrote, are what a story is made of.

3.title: The Fourth Estate Club
3.cn: 妮娅加入校报记者团，从一张照片、一次采访到一期特刊，逐渐理解“媒体”两个字的重量。

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · The Annual Issue
chapters.text:
Nia had never written for a **journal** before, so when the school's media **committee** **announce**d that the **annual** special issue needed a **photographer**, she signed up **joyfully**. The editor, Kai, was a **rare** **character**: **calm** under **pressure**, **flexible** with deadlines, and **entirely** without **emotion** when correcting an **error**.

"Every **entry** must **illustrate** one idea," Kai said. "We **publish** **throughout** the **region**, so **ensure** that nothing **affects** the **overall** tone." He gave her a **collection** of old issues, each with an **entertaining** **column**: a **novel** review, a **plot** summary of a **super** **soundtrack**, an interview with an **astronaut** about a **system** **crash**, and a report on a **disaster** in a **province** where a **flour** factory had burned.

The **journalist** in charge of the **subway** story had **average** **soccer** knowledge but a **horrible** sense of direction. "I **spot** the **custom** of the **ordinary** **female** fan," she said, "and then I **perceive** the **emotion** behind the **click**." Her **outline** was **broad** but **authority** on the subject was clear.

Nia needed **permission** to photograph a **civilization** exhibition, and the **nationality** of each **character** on display had to be **confirm**ed before **release**. She **breathe**d slowly, **merrily** humming to keep her **calm**, and set to work. **Innovation**, she decided, was not a **pack** of new gadgets but a way of seeing.

That night the paper went to press. A **medical** **team** arrived to **treat** a visitor who had fainted; the **committee** **confirm**ed the **entry** was **accurate**. "**Overall**," Kai said, "we have one **rare** **error**: the **astronaut**'s **nationality** is wrong in **column** three." Nia laughed, **joyfully** again. "At least the **photographer** got the **emotion** right," she said.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · The Journey of a T-shirt
chapters.text:
The second story began with a **guy** in a **gym** who **sweat**ed through his **jeans** and asked, "Where does a T-shirt come from?" Nia followed the trail: **cotton** fields, a **harvest** of **honey**-coloured **liquid**, a **flood** that ruined half the crop, and a **port** where **dozen**s of containers waited to be **export**ed.

"Every **quantity** has a **price**," said a worker at the **treatment** plant. "**Iron**, **wine**, **smog**, **insect**—everything **involve**s **profit** and **income**." He showed her how to **calculate** the **economic** cost of a single **application** of dye. "**Accurate** figures are **remarkable**," he said, "because most people **hesitate** to ask."

At the **discount** store, Nia watched a **majority** of shoppers **protest** about the **bitter** **flavour** of a new **roast** while others **slide** past **awkward**ly. A **bar** of soap, a **kit** for repairs, a **breath** of fresh air in the **smog**—the shop was a **habitat** for small decisions. "We **import** the **equipment**, we **replace** the labels, and we **certify** nothing," the owner admitted. "**Cash** is **advanced**, and the **operation** continues."

The **mission** was to **rescue** the truth from the marketing. Nia tracked an **overseas** **version** of the same shirt and found a **living** wage missing from the **slide** show. "The **economic** **benefit** is **specific**," her editor said, "but so is the **harm**." She wrote the final **chapter** by hand, and the **movement** of her pen felt like a small **protest** of its own.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · The Faces We Choose
chapters.text:
The third issue was about faces. On **campus**, Nia put a **sample** of photos on a **display** board and asked students to **react**. The **pattern** was **odd**: almost everyone chose the same **ideal** **profile**, a **delicate** **representation** that no **individual** actually matched.

"**Make-up** is a **practical** art," said one girl, **elegant** in a **metal**-framed mirror. "But the **trend** **stretch**es a **normal** face into a **shallow** **symbol**." A **broad** survey **enable**d Nia to **observe** how **gender** and **occupation** **vary** the **context** of beauty. "**Sex** sells, but **personality** **exist**s too," a boy said, and the **emphasis** shifted.

The **external** **impression** of a **generation** is **constantly** under **construction**. "We **ignore** the **effort** behind a **shave** or a **suit**," said a photographer, "and we **dive** into **hide-and-seek** with our own **image**." Her **duty**, she said, was to **carve** a **space** where a **wedding** photo and a **jogging** photo could sit side by side. "**Various** **branch**es of one **family**," she called them.

There was **relief** in the **mass** of replies, and a different **sort** of answer: **further** down the **column**, a **specific** **concept** appeared again and again — beauty is a **symbol** we **choose**, not a **rule** we **follow**. The **surround**ing **noise** of **make-up** ads **fade**d. Nia wrote the **highlight** of the issue: "**Nothing** about a face is **short-sighted**; only the way we look at it is."

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · A Tale from the South
chapters.text:
The final issue took Nia **further** than the **campus**. She won a **scholarship** to join a **conservation** **foundation** in Australia for a month — a **tough** **competition**, and a **specific** **qualification** in photography helped.

The flight **engine** hummed. She read the **guideline** for visitors and tried to **construct** a **diagram** of the trip. "**Seek** the **romantic** **highlight**, not the **extra** souvenir," Kai had said. "And **declare** nothing you cannot prove."

At the **foundation**, she met a **charitable** ranger who had spent a **decade** **employ**ing students to **track** **kangaroo**s. "**Recreation** and **conservation** can **compete**," he said, "but **sufficient** **enthusiasm** **persuade**s people to **engage**." He **employ**ed a **specific** **concept**: the **agricultural** **drought** had **harm**ed the **habitat**, and a **mosquito** **plague** followed.

She went **jogging** before dawn, then they drove the **highway** and saw a **deer**-like **dinosaur** of a machine, a **plate** of solar panels, and a **nearby** **studio** where an **opera** was being **postpone**d because of the heat. "**Anxious** tourists get **scared**," the ranger **calmly** said, "but a **dolphin** and a **whale** do not care about our schedule." Nia **revise**d her **chapter** that night: the **tale** would be about **movement**, not **escape**.

On the last day she watched a **flash** of lightning over the water and felt the **foundation** of her own **confidence** settle. The **recreation** of a **concept** she had once thought **romantic** — the wild — now had a **guideline** and a **qualification** attached. **Further** **effort**, she wrote, is the only **convincing** **chapter**.

4.title: The Chocolate Theory
4.cn: 艾薇的姑妈开巧克力店，她一边做“幸福”课题，一边在岛屿、网红与味觉之间寻找答案。

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · A Theory of Small Pleasures
chapters.text:
Ivy's aunt runs a chocolate shop in a **suburb** of the city. Every **item** in the **drawer** behind the counter has a story, and Ivy had heard them all. "People **associate** chocolate with happiness," her aunt said, "but that is a **theory**, not a **fact**."

Ivy was writing a **presentation** on happiness for her **nutrition** class. Her **tablet** was full of **scientific** **evidence**, yet the **overall** picture was **miserable**: a **decade** of studies, a **million** opinions. "**Lack** of sleep **affect**s **mood**," she read. "**Anxiety** and **depression** are not a **fashion**." The **chemical** **release** in the brain that chocolate **promote**s is real, but the **tone** of the ads **imply** that a **portion** can cure **cancer**.

"You **consume** a **calorie** and **afterwards** feel **disappointed**," her aunt said. "That is the **phenomenon**." She had a **solid** **recipe** for a **composition** of flavours, and she was **committed** to it. "**Self-reliance** and **discipline**," she said, "**persuade** people better than a **golf** **tournament** ever could."

At school, the class had to **wrestle** with a question: can **mutual** **cooperation** and **commitment** survive a **greedy** market? A **journalist** came to speak. "**Mostly**, the industry **adopt**s a **fry**-everything approach," she said. "**In contrast**, small shops **sacrifice** **profit** for **quality**." Her **urge** was for students to **appreciate** **essential**, **vital**, **crucial** things: sleep, **cycle** rides, a **poet**'s line, a friend's **tone** of voice.

"**Optimistic**?" the teacher asked. "**Incredibly**," Ivy said. She had **evidence**: a **consumption** study her aunt had **cooperate**d on suggested that a **mutual** **commitment** to small pleasures could **release** the **pressure** of a **depressed** **mood**. "**Abandon** the **fashion** of the big cure," she wrote. "Keep the small **essential**." The class clapped, and her aunt sent a box of **tablet**-shaped chocolates to celebrate.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · The Island That Kept Giving
chapters.text:
That summer Ivy joined a conservation camp on a **distant** island. The **tide** came in fast, the **wave**s broke over the **shelter**, and the **mosquito**es were **widespread**. "**Nevertheless**," the camp leader said, "we **preserve** what we can."

The island's **rural** **landscape** was a **plain** of **native** grass and **antique** walls. A **fellow** volunteer named Jun, who had been **nominate**d for a youth award, showed her a **visual** map of the **habitat**. "We cannot **predict** the **overflow** of the **tide**," he said, "but we can **defend** the **structure** of the **dormitory**."

A **victim** of the last flood became an **advocate** for the ban. **Anger** and **frustration** rose when a **campaign** to **ban** **garbage** near the **pub** was **skip**ped by the council. "**Inform** the **folk**," Jun said. "**Access** to clean water is a **responsibility**, not a favour."
